title: On Unlearning for Time-series Forecasting

paper.title: On Unlearning for Time-series Forecasting
paper.abstract:
Abstract Time-series forecasting is widely used in healthy, transportation, finance, and many other domains. Models in these settings are often trained on longitudinal user or entity level records, which may later require removal because they contain sensitive or proprietary information or have been corrupted by sensor failures. To address such deletion requests without costly retraining, machine unlearning has been widely studied as a practical mechanism for privacy protection and data governance. However, the application of machine unlearning to time series prediction has not yet been well realized, it mainly dues to the following unique challenges: Gradient-based unlearning can be unstable because a deleted observation participates in multiple causally connected forecasting windows, causing parameter updates to propagate beyond the requested interval and degrade retained forecasting utility.
Label-guided updating offers a more controlled alternative, but continuous and context-dependent forecasts lack a suitable replacement target, while the exact-retrained output is unavailable during unlearning. Moreover, the remaining support for a deleted temporal pattern is highly non-uniform. Some affected windows retain structurally similar counterparts in the retained data, whereas others
become underrepresented or isolated. We present RDTU , a R esidual D iffusion framework of T ime-series U nlearning that constructs labels without accessing an exact-retrained model at unlearning time. RDTU first uses a retained-set neural tangent kernel predictor to obtain a deletion-compatible base forecast. Then it quantifies the global and local structural support of each affected window using the volume contribution of the retained-reference data.
Conditioned on the query window, retained-set prediction, and structural support, a diffusion model generates a residual correction that estimates the counterfactual forecast, yielding a pseudo-label field that guides a lightweight model update. Experiments across real-world forecasting benchmarks show that RDTU consistently produces unlearned models that most closely match exact retraining among the evaluated efficient unlearning methods. It achieves this alignment while maintaining retained forecasting utility and reducing membership-inference signals.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Time-series forecasting has become a fundamental component of data-driven decision making across finance, healthcare, transportation, energy systems, and intelligent manufacturing, where historical observations are used to anticipate future risks, demands, and system states ( Lim and Zohren, 2021 ; Zonta et al., 2020 ; Mohapatra et al., 2024 ) . As forecasting models are trained on increasingly large and continuously collected data streams, they also face growing demands for selective data removal. In privacy-sensitive domains such as finance and healthcare, training sequences may contain sensitive personal information; under Article 17 of the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), data subjects may request the erasure of their personal data under specified conditions ( EU, 2016 ) . A parallel need arises in industrial monitoring, where sensor failures, calibration drift, and communication faults can introduce erroneous observations, while equipment aging can render previously collected operating patterns obsolete ( Teh et al., 2020 ; Goknil et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Once incorporated into model training, such observations may distort the learned temporal dependencies and compromise subsequent forecasts. To meet these deletion requirements, machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of designated training data from a trained model ( Cao and Yang, 2015 ; Wang et al., 2022 ) . Existing approaches are broadly divided into exact and approximate unlearning. Exact unlearning seeks to match the distribution of models retrained from scratch on the retained data, but often incurs prohibitive computational costs ( Ginart et al., 2019 ) . Approximate unlearning instead updates the original model to efficiently emulate this behavior. Gradient-ascent methods increase the forgetting-set loss, but their lack of an explicit convergence target can cause unstable optimization and severe utility degradation. NegGrad+ ( Kurmanji et al., 2023 ) and NPO ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) mitigate this problem by balancing gradients or bounding the forgetting objective. However, they primarily control how the model departs from forgotten samples rather than specifying its desired post-deletion behavior. This motivates label-based methods such as random labeling, which replace forgotten targets with constructed alternatives ( Graves et al., 2021 ; Di et al., 2026 ) . Methods developed for image and text unlearning do not transfer directly to time-series forecasting. Forecasting windows are ordered and extensively overlapping, so gradient ascent on forgotten windows may disrupt temporal representations shared with retained data. Label-based methods also lack a natural replacement target because arbitrary continuous values may violate temporal and cross-variable structures. Unlike classification labels or abstention responses ( Graves et al., 2021 ; Maini et al., 2024 ) , time series have no universal rejection label. TS-Unlearn addresses this problem by feeding Gaussian inputs into the original model to construct forgetting targets and dynamically balancing forgetting and retention ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . However, these targets are not conditioned on the specific query or its local support in the retained data. They constrain outputs to a plausible range but cannot approximate the predictions of exact unlearning. To address these challenges, we adopt label-based approximate unlearning and construct labels that approximate the predictions of exact unlearning for time-series forecasting. Because obtaining such labels directly would require retraining on the strictly retained set, we use a lightweight neural tangent kernel (NTK) predictor as an efficient regression surrogate. However, finite-width networks perform feature learning and nonlinear optimization, creating a non-negligible gap between their predictions and the NTK approximation. We therefore introduce training a small conditional diffusion model to learn the residual distribution between the trained model and its NTK predictor and transfer this residual pattern to retained-set conditions. To avoid conditioning on high-dimensional raw time-series windows, we further propose the structural irrelevance score (SIS), which summarizes complementary global directional change and local retained support. Conditioned on the retained-set NTK prediction and SIS, diffusion generates a residual correction that forms a suitable label for each affected window. Extensive experiments on univariate and multivariate datasets demonstrate a favorable balance among unlearning effectiveness, forecasting utility, and computational efficiency. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We formulate time-series forecasting unlearning under strict temporal deletion closure, which identifies all forecasting windows affected by a deletion request, and cast efficient approximate unlearning as the construction of counterfactual labels that approximate the predictions of an exact-retrained model. • We introduce the Structural Irreplaceability Score (SIS), which complements the model-dependent NTK prediction by quantifying the global and local structural support of each affected window. SIS provides a compact condition for residual generation and reduces reliance on costly raw-window representations. • We propose RDTU , a label-guided Residual Diffusion framework that combines a retained-set NTK predictor with a simple conditional residual diffusion model. The NTK predictor provides a lightweight counterfactual base prediction, while the diffusion model compensates for the substantial finite-width discrepancy between the NTK approximation and the corresponding trained neural predictor.

sections.heading: 2.2 Time-series Exact Unlearning and Approximate Unlearning
sections.text: Consider an unlearning request for a contiguous temporal interval 𝕋 f = [ t i , t s ) {\mathbb{T}}_{\mathrm{f}}=[t_{\mathrm{i}},t_{\mathrm{s}}) in the original time series. The request asks the model to forget the training influence of the observations x t i , x t i + 1 , … , x t s − 1 {x_{t_{\mathrm{i}}},x_{t_{\mathrm{i}}+1},\ldots,x_{t_{\mathrm{s}}-1}} . For time-series forecasting, this unlearning request cannot be handled by simply removing the training windows whose prediction targets lie inside 𝕋 f {\mathbb{T}}_{\mathrm{f}} . Each supervised window contains both an input context and a future prediction target. Therefore, an observation in 𝕋 f {\mathbb{T}}_{\mathrm{f}} may appear as the target of one training window, while also appearing as part of the input context of several subsequent windows. For a forecasting sample ( 𝒙 t , 𝒚 t ) ({\bm{x}}_{t},{\bm{y}}_{t}) , its complete temporal footprint is 𝕀 t = [ t − ℓ , t + h ) {\mathbb{I}}_{t}=[t-\ell,t+h) , which includes its input interval [ t − ℓ , t ) [t-\ell,t) and target interval [ t , t + h ) [t,t+h) . We regard a sample as affected by the deletion request whenever any part of its temporal footprint overlaps the requested interval: 𝒟 f ​ ( 𝕋 f ) = { ( 𝒙 t , 𝒚 t ) ∈ 𝒟 | 𝕀 t ∩ 𝕋 f ≠ ∅ } . \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{f}}({\mathbb{T}}_{\mathrm{f}})=\left\{({\bm{x}}_{t},{\bm{y}}_{t})\in\mathcal{D}\;\middle|\;{\mathbb{I}}_{t}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\mathrm{f}}\neq\varnothing\right\}. sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Proposed Approach Overview. To achieve the approximate unlearning of time series, we propose RDTU , a R esidual D iffusion framework of T ime-series U nlearning. As illustrated in Figure 1 , the overall method consists of four main components. First, a retained-set neural tangent kernel (NTK) predictor provides a deletion-compatible base prediction that enables an approximation of the target exact unlearning model. Second, the Structural Irreplaceability Score (SIS) complements the influence estimation by quantifying the global and local structural support provided by each closure window, thereby characterizing the extent to which the unlearned data are replaceable for prediction. Third, conditioned on the NTK prediction and the SIS-based valuation of the forgetting windows, a diffusion model learns the residual between the NTK prediction and the model prediction, generating a refined label field for unlearning. Finally, the generated label field guides the unlearning update, enabling effective removal of the forgetting windows while preserving forecasting performance on strictly retained windows. Figure 1: Overview of our proposed time-series unlearning framework RDTU. (1) The retained-set NTK predictor produces a base prediction for the affected window. (2) SIS integrates global directional contribution and local retained support to quantify the structural irreplaceability. (3) Conditioned on the NTK prediction and SIS, the residual diffusion model generates a residual correction. (4) The final label guides the unlearning update.

sections.heading: 3.1 NTK Predictor Based Label Construction
sections.text: Random labeling provides a practical route for approximate unlearning: rather than preserving the original targets of deleted samples, the unlearned model is guided toward constructed targets that reflect the desired post-deletion behaviour. In categorical tasks, such targets are usually formed by replacing the ground-truth label with an alternative label or a prescribed distribution ( Chundawat et al., 2023 ; Di et al., 2026 ) . This option is not directly available for time-series forecasting, where each target is a continuous future trajectory whose value is correlated to its temporal context. Assigning an arbitrary value, such as zero or a retained target, does not in general represent the prediction of a model that has never been trained on the deleted interval. Follow the definition of approaximate unlearning in Section 2.2 , the ideal label for each closure window should be the prediction of the exact-unlearned model. Obtaining 𝒚 t ∗ {\bm{y}}_{t}^{*} from exact unlearned model incurs the substantial computational cost. Therefore, we constructed an NTK predictor as a basic predictor that can be processed, in order to closely approximate our target model with lower cost. Their difference is the initialization residual. The ridge coefficient stabilizes the regression. For computational efficiency, we approximate these kernel quantities using Nyström features ( Williams and Seeger, 2000 ) , avoiding construction of the full empirical NTK matrix while preserving the same kernel-ridge objective. However, the NTK predictor provides only a linearized approximation of neural-network training. It cannot fully capture finite-width feature learning, nonlinear parameter interactions, or the stochastic optimization dynamics of the actual model ( Chizat et al., 2019 ; Yang and Hu, 2021 ) . Consequently, its predictions exhibit a substantial and non-negligible discrepancy from those of the trained neural predictor. For the original model and its corresponding NTK predictor, we define this prediction gap as the residual: 𝑹 t 𝒟 = f 𝜽 ∗ ​ ( 𝒙 t ) − g 𝒟 ​ ( 𝒙 t ) . {\bm{R}}_{t}^{\mathcal{D}}=f_{{\bm{\theta}}^{*}}\left({\bm{x}}_{t}\right)-g_{\mathcal{D}}\left({\bm{x}}_{t}\right). (14) A straightforward approach to residual correction is to fit a deterministic regressor between the available conditions and the residuals. However, such methods impose a restricted functional form and generally produce only a point estimate, which may be insufficient for capturing nonlinear or heteroscedastic. We therefore employ a conditional diffusion model to learn the distribution of residual corrections. Importantly, this construction is agnostic to the architecture of the original forecasting model. It does not require access to model-specific hidden representations, gradients, or parameter structures, but relies on the NTK prediction and the features of the corresponding data. The source residual defined in Equation 14 provides supervision for this process, enabling the diffusion model to capture the finite-width discrepancy between the trained neural predictor and its NTK approximation. sections.text: Training diffusion on raw data is highly expensive, with costs comparable to retraining on the retained set. Using raw data as the conditional input for the diffusion model is to extract the features of the corresponding data and generate the corresponding residual values. Since the NTK prediction values have to some extent already reflected the impact of this data on the entire model, we introduce the Structural Irreplaceability Score (SIS), a compact reference-based descriptor that quantifies how difficult each closure query is to replace using the available reference patterns. SIS combines a global criterion and a local criterion to measure the replaceability of data. We quantify global replaceability by measuring the change of Volume value in the directional structure of the reference dataset induced by a closure query. Each forecasting window is first converted into a standardized vector representation ϕ t = 𝒙 t \bm{\phi}_{t}={\bm{x}}_{t} . Updating the model with such constructed targets is conceptually aligned with label-based and teacher-based unlearning strategies, which redirect the predictions of affected samples while preserving useful knowledge learned from the retained data ( Chundawat et al., 2023 ; Kurmanji et al., 2023 ; Graves et al., 2021 ) . In our setting, the labels are generated from retained-set information and are used to update the original model. We initialize the unlearned model from the original parameters 𝜽 u ( 0 ) = 𝜽 ∗ {\bm{\theta}}_{\mathrm{u}}^{(0)}={\bm{\theta}}^{*} . sections.heading: 4.1 Datasets and Experimental Setups
sections.text: Datasets. We conduct experiments on four public time-series datasets. Air Quality ( Chen, 2017 ) and Traffic ( Lai et al., 2018 ) are used for univariate forecasting, whereas EEG ( Zyma et al., 2019 ) and HAR70+ ( Logacjov and Ustad, 2023 ) are used for multivariate forecasting. For each dataset, we select 10 series or subjects and train a separate forecasting model for each one. Each model is evaluated under three deletion seeds, yielding 30 deletion requests per dataset. We first average the results across deletion seeds for each series or subject and then report the macro-average across the 10 series or subjects. Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate unlearning effectiveness using membership indistinguishability ( Shokri et al., 2017 ; Carlini et al., 2022 ) and functional agreement with exact retraining. The former is measured by the two-sided U/N AUC, where values closer to 0.5 0.5 indicate stronger forgetting. The latter is measured by the F-P Gap, namely the normalized RMSE between unlearned and exact-retrained predictions on forgetting inputs, reported as a percentage. Forecasting utility is evaluated using test NRMSE, while computational efficiency is measured by wall-clock time. Detailed metric and timing implementations are provided in the Appendix. Baselines. We compare our model against a sizable collection of representative baselines: SSD ( Foster et al., 2024 ) , NegGrad+ ( Kurmanji et al., 2023 ) , Random label , Zero label , SCRUB-R ( Kurmanji et al., 2023 ) , TS Unlearn ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , and we use the Transformer ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) as our base model. The details are described in the Appendix.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduced RDTU, a label-guided framework for approximate unlearning in time-series forecasting. RDTU provides an efficient prediction by constructing an NTK predictor, and the structural irrelevance score is used to characterize the global and local support conditions of each affected window. Conditional residual diffusion subsequently corrects the discrepancy between the NTK approximation and the corresponding neural predictor, and the resulting labels guide a lightweight unlearning update. Experiments on four univariate and multivariate forecasting benchmarks show that RDTU achieves the lowest F-P Gap and test NRMSE among the evaluated efficient unlearning methods, while maintaining low membership distinguishability and requiring substantially less computation than exact retraining.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work investigates machine unlearning as a means of reducing the influence of designated observations on time-series forecasting models. All experiments use existing publicly available benchmark datasets; no new participants were recruited, and no new personal data were collected. The EEG and HAR datasets contain previously collected human-subject measurements, and this study uses only the publicly released research data. RDTU provides approximate rather than certified unlearning and should not be interpreted as offering a formal or legal guarantee of data erasure. Its effectiveness depends on the adopted threat model, evaluation protocol, and deployment setting. Applications in privacy-sensitive domains should therefore incorporate appropriate access controls, deletion audits, and regulatory review. Moreover, deletion requests and model updates should be documented and independently auditable to prevent unlearning techniques from being misused to obscure data provenance or selectively manipulate model behaviour.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: To support reproducibility, all methods were tested using the same preprocessing, data partitioning, deletion requests, and evaluation procedures. The detailed experimental configurations and implementation methods are listed in the appendix. For each dataset, we evaluated 10 sequences or subjects under three deletion seeds, averaged the results for each sequence or subject under different seeds, and then reported the corresponding macro average. The source code, configuration files, selected sequence or subject identifiers, and random seeds will be included in the supplementary materials. The published content will include scripts for training the original model and re-training the precise model, as well as scripts for executing our experiments.

sections.heading: A.1 Datasets
sections.text: We conduct experiments on four public time-series datasets. Air Quality and Traffic are used for univariate forecasting, whereas EEG and HAR70+ are used for multivariate forecasting. The forecasting horizon is one time step for all datasets. For each dataset, we select 10 series or subjects and train a separate forecasting model for each one. Each model is evaluated under three deletion seeds, yielding 30 deletion requests per dataset. We first average the results across deletion seeds for each series or subject and then report the macro-average across the 10 series or subjects.A deletion request is specified as a contiguous block of raw observations. We remove every forecasting example whose input or prediction target overlaps this block, thereby enforcing strict temporal deletion closure. Below, the input-window length denotes the number of historical observations provided to the forecasting model, while the deletion-block length denotes the number of consecutive raw observations selected for forgetting. • Air Quality : This dataset contains hourly air-pollutant and meteorological measurements collected from 12 monitoring sites in Beijing between March 2013 and February 2017 ( Chen, 2017 ) . We treat the PM 2.5 measurements from each site as an independent univariate time series and predict its concentration at the next time step. We use an input window of 24 hourly observations. • Traffic : This dataset contains hourly road occupancy measurements from 862 freeway sensors in the San Francisco Bay Area during 2015–2016 ( Lai et al., 2018 ) . We treat each sensor as an independent univariate time series and predict its occupancy rate at the next time step. We use an input window of 16 hourly observations. • EEG : The EEGMAT dataset contains 19-channel EEG recordings from 36 subjects performing mental arithmetic tasks, sampled at 500 Hz ( Zyma et al., 2019 ) . We use the Fp1, Fp2, and F3 channels and jointly predict their values at the next time step. We use an input window of 32 samples. • HAR70+ : This dataset contains accelerometer recordings from 18 older adults wearing tri-axial sensors on the lower back and thigh, sampled at 50 Hz ( Logacjov and Ustad, 2023 ) . We use the back_y , thigh_x , and thigh_y channels and jointly predict their values at the next time step. We use an input window of 32 samples.

sections.heading: A.3 Conditional Residual Diffusion
sections.text: RDTU does not directly apply diffusion to the forecasting targets. Instead, it models the discrepancy between a trained forecasting model and its corresponding NTK predictor. This design separates the counterfactual label into an NTK-based prediction and a residual correction. The NTK predictor provides the principal prediction under a given reference dataset, while the diffusion model captures the finite-width and nonlinear effects that cannot be represented by the NTK approximation.

(35) The input window remains unchanged because it specifies the query for which the counterfactual label is required. In contrast, g 𝒟 r ​ ( 𝒙 t ) g_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{r}}}({\bm{x}}_{t}) represents the prediction supported by the strictly retained set, and s t 𝒟 r s_{t}^{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{r}}} measures the structural change caused by adding the closure query to that set. sections.heading: A.5 Metrics
sections.text: To evaluate unlearning effectiveness , we consider both membership indistinguishability and functional agreement with exact retraining. Membership indistinguishability is measured by the two-sided U/N AUC, defined as max ⁡ { a , 1 − a } \max\{a,1-a\} , where a a is the ROC AUC for distinguishing forgotten samples ( U U ) from never-seen samples ( N N ). A value closer to 0.5 0.5 indicates that the forgotten samples are less distinguishable from non-members. Functional agreement is measured by the F-P Gap, defined as the RMSE between the predictions of the unlearned model and those of the exact-retraining model on the forgetting inputs, normalized by the standard deviation of the raw training targets and reported as a percentage. A lower F-P Gap indicates closer agreement with exact retraining. To evaluate forecasting utility , we report the test NRMSE, computed as the test RMSE divided by the standard deviation of the raw training series before deletion, where a lower value indicates better predictive performance. Computational efficiency is measured by the wall-clock time required to complete each unlearning method. For our method, the reported time includes NTK computation, diffusion training and sampling, and model updating. Membership Inference Attack We conduct the membership audit at the level of temporal deletion units rather than isolated observations. An audit candidate may therefore contain multiple forecasting windows induced by the same temporal interval. Following the strict temporal deletion closure defined in Equation 2 , we define the closure operator for an arbitrary temporal interval 𝕋 ′ {\mathbb{T}}^{\prime} as 𝒞 ( 𝕋 ′ ) = { ( 𝒙 t , 𝒚 t ) | 𝕀 t ∩ 𝕋 ′ ≠ ∅ } , 𝕀 t = [ t − ℓ , t + h ) . \mathcal{C}\left({\mathbb{T}}^{\prime}\right)=\left\{({\bm{x}}_{t},{\bm{y}}_{t})\;\middle|\;{\mathbb{I}}_{t}\cap{\mathbb{T}}^{\prime}\neq\emptyset\right\},\qquad{\mathbb{I}}_{t}=[t-\ell,t+h). (38) Let 𝕋 f {\mathbb{T}}_{\mathrm{f}} denote the raw timestamps included in a deletion request, and let 𝕋 n {\mathbb{T}}_{\mathrm{n}} denote an equally sized set of timestamps held out before the original model is trained. The forgotten and never-seen audit collections are defined as 𝒜 U = 𝒞 ⁡ ( 𝕋 f ) , 𝒜 N = 𝒞 ⁡ ( 𝕋 n ) . \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{U}}=\mathcal{C}\left({\mathbb{T}}_{\mathrm{f}}\right),\qquad\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{N}}=\mathcal{C}\left({\mathbb{T}}_{\mathrm{n}}\right). (39) Thus, 𝒜 U \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{U}} contains every forecasting window whose input context or prediction target overlaps the requested deletion interval. These windows were used to train the original model f 𝜽 𝒟 ∗ f_{{\bm{\theta}}_{\mathcal{D}}^{*}} but should behave as non-members after unlearning. In contrast, 𝒜 N \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{N}} is excluded before the original model is trained and therefore consists of genuine non-members. The never-seen intervals are fixed for each user across deletion seeds, whereas the forgotten intervals are independently sampled for each deletion request. We additionally select a retained-member audit collection 𝒜 M ⊂ 𝒟 r \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{M}}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{r}} . To reduce distributional bias, candidates in 𝒜 M \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{M}} and 𝒜 N \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{N}} are matched to those in 𝒜 U \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{U}} using temporal descriptors and Hungarian matching. The resulting M/U/N groups are mutually disjoint and contain the same number of temporal audit units. For multivariate data, all variables observed within the same temporal window are jointly treated as one forecasting sample rather than as independent membership candidates.

sections.text: We implement membership inference using candidate-conditioned LiRA. For each temporal audit unit i i , shadow models are trained using the same background training data while alternately including or excluding that candidate. Because one candidate may induce multiple closure windows, the forecasting statistics over all its associated windows are aggregated into a single attack-feature vector 𝒛 i ​ ( f ) {\bm{z}}_{i}(f) . The feature vector contains squared error, absolute error, signed error, residual variation, prediction statistics, and target statistics. Using the outputs of the shadow models, we fit separate diagonal Gaussian distributions to the observations obtained when candidate i i is included in or excluded from shadow-model training: p c , i = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝝁 i c , diag ⁡ ( ( 𝝈 i c ) 2 ) ) , c ∈ { in , out } . p_{c,i}=\mathcal{N}\left(\bm{\mu}_{i}^{c},\operatorname{diag}\left(\left(\bm{\sigma}_{i}^{c}\right)^{2}\right)\right),\qquad c\in\left\{\mathrm{in},\mathrm{out}\right\}. (40) For a target forecasting model f 𝜽 f_{{\bm{\theta}}} , the candidate-conditioned LiRA score is the log-likelihood ratio s i LiRA ​ ( f 𝜽 ) = log ⁡ p in , i ​ ( 𝒛 i ​ ( f 𝜽 ) ) − log ⁡ p out , i ​ ( 𝒛 i ​ ( f 𝜽 ) ) . s_{i}^{\mathrm{LiRA}}\left(f_{{\bm{\theta}}}\right)=\log p_{\mathrm{in},i}\left({\bm{z}}_{i}\left(f_{{\bm{\theta}}}\right)\right)-\log p_{\mathrm{out},i}\left({\bm{z}}_{i}\left(f_{{\bm{\theta}}}\right)\right). (41) A larger score indicates that the behavior of candidate i i is more consistent with that of a training member. When auditing the original model f 𝜽 𝒟 ∗ f_{{\bm{\theta}}_{\mathcal{D}}^{*}} , both 𝒜 M \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{M}} and 𝒜 U \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{U}} are treated as members, whereas 𝒜 N \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{N}} is treated as the non-member group. When auditing the unlearned model f 𝜽 u f_{{\bm{\theta}}_{\mathrm{u}}} , only 𝒜 M \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{M}} retain member-like behavior, while candidates in both 𝒜 U \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{U}} and 𝒜 N \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{N}} should exhibit non-member behavior. sections.heading: A.6 Baselines
sections.text: We compare RDTU with the following representative unlearning baselines. Original denotes the forecasting model before unlearning, while Retrain trains the same architecture from scratch on the strictly retained set and serves as the exact-unlearning reference. SSD ( Foster et al., 2024 ) uses Fisher information to identify parameters disproportionately associated with the forgetting set and selectively dampens them. NegGrad+ ( Kurmanji et al., 2023 ) combines gradient ascent on the forgetting set with gradient descent on the retained set. Zero-label replaces the targets of affected windows with zero vectors, whereas Random-label assigns randomly generated continuous targets following the random-labeling strategy. SCRUB-R ( Kurmanji et al., 2023 ) adopts a teacher–student framework that moves the student away from the original model on the forgetting set while preserving its predictions on the retained set. TS-Unlearn ( Wang et al., 2026 ) constructs replacement targets by feeding Gaussian noise into the original model and dynamically balances the forgetting and retention objectives through Pareto optimization.

sections.heading: D.1 Computational scalability
sections.text: Although RDTU is more efficient than exact retraining, its computational cost may increase for long sequences, high-dimensional multivariate data, and large forecasting architectures. In particular, empirical NTK construction requires computing and storing parameter-gradient features for numerous forecasting windows, while residual generation involves multiple denoising steps for every affected query. Future work could reduce these costs through incremental Nystr”om approximation, low-rank kernel representations, and cached NTK features that can be reused across deletion requests. The retained-reference statistics required by SIS could likewise be updated incrementally instead of being recomputed after each deletion. On the diffusion side, accelerated or distilled samplers, batched residual generation, and adaptive denoising schedules could further reduce inference time. For example, queries with strong retained support could use fewer denoising steps, whereas structurally irreplaceable queries with high SIS values could receive additional computation. A comprehensive scalability study should separately report one-time preprocessing costs, per-request latency, peak memory consumption, and amortized runtime as the number of windows, variables, deletion requests, and diffusion steps increases.

sections.heading: D.2 Broader evaluation and stronger guarantees
sections.text: Future evaluations should examine RDTU under a broader range of forecasting and deletion conditions. Relevant settings include longer forecasting horizons, higher-dimensional multivariate series, irregular sampling, missing observations, temporal distribution shifts, and deletion intervals spanning rare or rapidly changing patterns. It would also be valuable to vary the deletion ratio, interval length, and number of sequential requests to determine when the residual-transfer assumption begins to deteriorate. Evaluations with recurrent networks, temporal convolutional networks, Transformers, and state-space models would further assess the generality of the architecture-agnostic design. In addition, the current evaluation measures empirical agreement with exact retraining and resistance to membership inference, but these results do not provide a formal guarantee of data removal. Future studies should consider adaptive black-box and white-box attacks that exploit model outputs, gradients, parameters, or intermediate representations, together with reconstruction and model-inversion attacks. A complementary theoretical direction is to bound the discrepancy between the unlearned and exact-retrained models in terms of the NTK approximation error, residual-generation error, and optimization error. Such analyses could support verifiable stopping criteria or certified variants of RDTU for deployment in privacy-sensitive applications.

Models in these settings are often trained on longitudinal user or entity level records, which may later require removal because they contain sensitive or proprietary information or have been corrupted by sensor failures. To address such deletion requests without costly retraining, machine unlearning has been widely studied as a practical mechanism for privacy protection and data governance. However, the application of machine unlearning to time series prediction has not yet been well realized, it mainly dues to the following unique challenges: Gradient-based unlearning can be unstable because a deleted observation participates in multiple causally connected forecasting windows, causing parameter updates to propagate beyond the requested interval and degrade retained forecasting utility. Label-guided updating offers a more controlled alternative, but continuous and context-dependent forecasts lack a suitable replacement target, while the exact-retrained output is unavailable during unlearning. Moreover, the remaining support for a deleted temporal pattern is highly non-uniform. Some affected windows retain structurally similar counterparts in the retained data, whereas others become underrepresented or isolated. We present RDTU , a R esidual D iffusion framework of T ime-series U nlearning that constructs labels without accessing an exact-retrained model at unlearning time. RDTU first uses a retained-set neural tangent kernel predictor to obtain a deletion-compatible base forecast. Then it quantifies the global and local structural support of each affected window using the volume contribution of the retained-reference data. Conditioned on the query window, retained-set prediction, and structural support, a diffusion model generates a residual correction that estimates the counterfactual forecast, yielding a pseudo-label field that guides a lightweight model update. Experiments across real-world forecasting benchmarks show that RDTU consistently produces unlearned models that most closely match exact retraining among the evaluated efficient unlearning methods. It achieves this alignment while maintaining retained forecasting utility and reducing membership-inference signals. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 2 2 footnotetext: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Time-series forecasting has become a fundamental component of data-driven decision making across finance, healthcare, transportation, energy systems, and intelligent manufacturing, where historical observations are used to anticipate future risks, demands, and system states ( Lim and Zohren, 2021 ; Zonta et al., 2020 ; Mohapatra et al., 2024 ) . As forecasting models are trained on increasingly large and continuously collected data streams, they also face growing demands for selective data removal. In privacy-sensitive domains such as finance and healthcare, training sequences may contain sensitive personal information; under Article 17 of the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), data subjects may request the erasure of their personal data under specified conditions ( EU, 2016 ) . A parallel need arises in industrial monitoring, where sensor failures, calibration drift, and communication faults can introduce erroneous observations, while equipment aging can render previously collected operating patterns obsolete ( Teh et al., 2020 ; Goknil et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Once incorporated into model training, such observations may distort the learned temporal dependencies and compromise subsequent forecasts. To meet these deletion requirements, machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of designated training data from a trained model ( Cao and Yang, 2015 ; Wang et al., 2022 ) . Existing approaches are broadly divided into exact and approximate unlearning. Exact unlearning seeks to match the distribution of models retrained from scratch on the retained data, but often incurs prohibitive computational costs ( Ginart et al., 2019 ) . Approximate unlearning instead updates the original model to efficiently emulate this behavior. Gradient-ascent methods increase the forgetting-set loss, but their lack of an explicit convergence target can cause unstable optimization and severe utility degradation. NegGrad+ ( Kurmanji et al., 2023 ) and NPO ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) mitigate this problem by balancing gradients or bounding the forgetting objective. However, they primarily control how the model departs from forgotten samples rather than specifying its desired post-deletion behavior. This motivates label-based methods such as random labeling, which replace forgotten targets with constructed alternatives ( Graves et al., 2021 ; Di et al., 2026 ) . Methods developed for image and text unlearning do not transfer directly to time-series forecasting. Forecasting windows are ordered and extensively overlapping, so gradient ascent on forgotten windows may disrupt temporal representations shared with retained data. Label-based methods also lack a natural replacement target because arbitrary continuous values may violate temporal and cross-variable structures. Unlike classification labels or abstention responses ( Graves et al., 2021 ; Maini et al., 2024 ) , time series have no universal rejection label. TS-Unlearn addresses this problem by feeding Gaussian inputs into the original model to construct forgetting targets and dynamically balancing forgetting and retention ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . However, these targets are not conditioned on the specific query or its local support in the retained data. They constrain outputs to a plausible range but cannot approximate the predictions of exact unlearning. To address these challenges, we adopt label-based approximate unlearning and construct labels that approximate the predictions of exact unlearning for time-series forecasting. Because obtaining such labels directly would require retraining on the strictly retained set, we use a lightweight neural tangent kernel (NTK) predictor as an efficient regression surrogate. However, finite-width networks perform feature learning and nonlinear optimization, creating a non-negligible gap between their predictions and the NTK approximation. We therefore introduce training a small conditional diffusion model to learn the residual distribution between the trained model and its NTK predictor and transfer this residual pattern to retained-set conditions. To avoid conditioning on high-dimensional raw time-series windows, we further propose the structural irrelevance score (SIS), which summarizes complementary global directional change and local retained support. Conditioned on the retained-set NTK prediction and SIS, diffusion generates a residual correction that forms a suitable label for each affected window. Extensive experiments on univariate and multivariate datasets demonstrate a favorable balance among unlearning effectiveness, forecasting utility, and computational efficiency. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We formulate time-series forecasting unlearning under strict temporal deletion closure, which identifies all forecasting windows affected by a deletion request, and cast efficient approximate unlearning as the construction of counterfactual labels that approximate the predictions of an exact-retrained model. • We introduce the Structural Irreplaceability Score (SIS), which complements the model-dependent NTK prediction by quantifying the global and local structural support of each affected window. SIS provides a compact condition for residual generation and reduces reliance on costly raw-window representations. • We propose RDTU , a label-guided Residual Diffusion framework that combines a retained-set NTK predictor with a simple conditional residual diffusion model. The NTK predictor provides a lightweight counterfactual base prediction, while the diffusion model compensates for the substantial finite-width discrepancy between the NTK approximation and the corresponding trained neural predictor. 2 Problem Definition and Related Works 2.1 Sliding-Window Forecasting Let { x 1 , … , x i , … , x T } \{x_{1},\ldots,x_{i},\ldots,x_{T}\} denote the observed time series to train a forecasting model 1 1 1 We focus on univariate data to simplify notation, and the concepts can be extended to multivariate ones. . As illustrated in Figure 1 , the overall method consists of four main components. First, a retained-set neural tangent kernel (NTK) predictor provides a deletion-compatible base prediction that enables an approximation of the target exact unlearning model. Second, the Structural Irreplaceability Score (SIS) complements the influence estimation by quantifying the global and local structural support provided by each closure window, thereby characterizing the extent to which the unlearned data are replaceable for prediction. Finally, the generated label field guides the unlearning update, enabling effective removal of the forgetting windows while preserving forecasting performance on strictly retained windows.
